extracted.intended_audience: judges, lawyers, forensic psychologists, and legal scholars evaluating testimony and evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for assessing witnesses, testimony, perception, memory, and evidential weight in legal contexts; covers perceptual limitations, memory, inference, expert testimony, corroboration, and procedural organization of a case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue must be defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue, must be defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear definition of the legal issue is required (see p.11). Properly defining the issue is a prerequisite for organizing and evaluating evidence and testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation of case
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisation, of case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases must be organized (see p.12) so that relevant evidence and central questions are separated from side-issues; succession/order of facts is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuation, of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the various sources and relative importance of evidence when assessing a case (see p.12). Consider corroboration and relevance; beware of irrelevant circumstances to proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources, various, of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and weigh different sources (e.g., servants, promoters, inventors) and understand their tendencies to mislead or to be informative (see p.12, p.63).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation of conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for changes in conditions under which observations were made, as these affect perception and reliability of testimony (see p.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation as corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation, as corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent observations should be used to corroborate testimony (see p.55); use observation differences as checks on claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training of witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Training, of witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses may be trained or untrained; training affects perception and reporting (see p.16). Consider how instruction/public education influence understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts as witnesses and their fallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts, are human; their opinion of judiciary; and rules of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts' testimony must be examined critically—experts are fallible and bring biases; consider their relation with judges and jurymen, and how expert perception differs from lay perception (see p.14, p.229).

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness demeanor categories (wordy/laconic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses, wandering of, wordy, laconic; method of drawing out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify witness style (wandering, wordy, laconic) and employ suitable methods to elicit reliable information (see pp.17–20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Witnesses do not know what they know
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses, do not know what they know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses may lack awareness of the relevance or content of their own knowledge; interviewers must draw out latent information (see p.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officials may impose on witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials, impose on witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to how officials' conduct or questioning can shape or induce testimony (see p.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind acceptance of testimony is hazardous
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony, blind acceptance of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid accepting testimony without critical evaluation and corroboration (see p.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions and interpretation of testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony, contradictions in; interpretation of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify contradictions and interpret their origin (error, illusion, misperception); resolve by cross-checking facts and context (see p.108).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training/education affects difficulty of eliciting truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty with educated witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educated witnesses may be more difficult to draw out; adapt questioning techniques accordingly (see p.23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest and attention as determinants of reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest, importance in judge and expert; how aroused in witnesses; and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aroused interest and attention influence perception and memory; evaluate whether a witness was sufficiently attentive and interested (see pp.37–39).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatigue, time of day, and misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Fatigue, and misunderstanding; Time, of day and mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fatigue and time variables impair perception and memory and can cause verbal misunderstandings; consider timing when assessing testimony (see pp.245, 473).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intoxication and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Intoxication; and responsibility; and theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for intoxication’s effects on perception, memory, and responsibility when weighing testimony or confessions (see pp.484–488).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confessions: risk of false confessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Confession and secrets; confessions may be false due to disease, dreams, toxication, coercion, or priestly pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate confessions critically—false confessions can arise from pathology, suggestion, desire for absolution, or coercion (see pp.29–31 and footnotes [58],[63]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory: reproduction and time factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory; and reproduction; and time; theories of memory; rules for helping recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess memory reliability by considering time elapsed, activity-related proportionate memory, reproduction techniques, locality, and known peculiarities (see pp.258–269). Apply rules for assisting recollection cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions and their classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Illusions, of memory; classification of; limits of; optical, auditory, tactual, taste, olfactory; reasons for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate illusions (optical, auditory, tactual, gustatory, olfactory) from false inferences; understand causes and limits to determine whether a witness experienced an illusion (see pp.424–456).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception: purity, limits, and influence of training/environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception, purity of; visual; limitations; influence of environment and training; how to test differences; of experts; subconscious; orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge perceptual testimony with awareness of perceptual limitations, effects of training and environment, expert vs lay perceptual differences, and subconscious influences; use tests to probe differences (see pp.187–231).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and speed as tests of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition; Speed, a test of knowledge; unit-characters; variety of recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition performance and reaction speed as indicators of knowledge or familiarity (see pp.221–233).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual perception specifics: binocular, form, size, perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual perception, binocular; and form; and size; perspective; position of lines influences size; orifice effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for visual factors (binocular vision, form perception, size/position/perspective distortions, occlusions) when evaluating visual identifications (see pp.201–204, 427–431).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactile and other senses: interrelation and illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch; tests sense of sight; relation to other senses; influence of drugs; transpositions of skin; wetness; bodily sensitiveness; illusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tactile evidence and the interplay of senses, drug effects, and known tactile illusions when assessing testimony based on touch (see pp.215–220, 449).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and gesture as corroborative signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Timbre, vocal, influence of emotions on, corroborative value; Gesture, importance and relation to voice; Gesticulation observation compared with writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe vocal qualities and gestures as supplementary corroborative cues, but evaluate them in context and with knowledge of variability and possible misinterpretation (see pp.43–49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal equation and individual differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal equation, the; differences in observation; isolated influences; subconscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account individual biases and systematic personal differences in perception and reporting when comparing testimonies (see pp.121, 376, 245).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudices, prepossession, and egoism affecting testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudices; prepossession; egoism and veracity; egoism a criterion of veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess witnesses for prejudices, prepossessions, and egoistic motives which may skew truthfulness; egoism can be both a sign and a confound of veracity (see pp.412–414, 28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability, repetition, rules, and legal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability; increases through repetition; conditioned and unconditioned; value of; rule and exceptions; probability and criminal procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use probabilistic reasoning (repetition increases probability) carefully in legal contexts; understand conditioned vs unconditioned probabilities and how legal rules interpret 'proved' as high probability (see pp.131–158, 143).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction and inference: sources of mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction; and the lawyer; difficulties; leaps in inference; origin of mistakes in inference; false inference compared with illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize inductive reasoning and inferences made by witnesses and experts for leaps, aprioristic errors, analogy misuse, and other reasoning mistakes (see pp.137–176, 425).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aprioristic statutes and preconceived rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes, aprioristic; Rule, and exceptions; and probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of aprioristic rules and statutes that may bias legal reasoning; weigh exceptions and empirical probability (see pp.5, 134, 158).

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-issues vs central issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Side-issues, confused with central ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish peripheral matters from central facts of the case to avoid distraction and misvaluation of evidence (see p.116).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age, senility, children, and their specific memory/perception traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduction of children and aged; memory of idiots; senility in witnesses; peculiarities of recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust expectations for reliability depending on age and cognitive status—children, the aged, and the mentally impaired show distinct memory and perceptual patterns (see pp.270–276, 372–375).

rubrics_metrics.name: Women as witnesses: claimed general tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Woman—status, defined by function; testimony of women; emotionalism; weakness; differences from men; crimes of women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists many claimed differences in women’s testimony and character (e.g., emotionalism, punctuality, conservatism). If used, these generalizations must be scrutinized for bias and empirical support (see pp.300–364).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs and uneducated judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs, judgment of the uneducated on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when relying on laypersons’ interpretations of photographs; training and education alter judgment (see p.390).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value of bodily signs (tears, fainting, smiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tears, fainting, smile, paleness, hair rising—signs described; resolution importance as sign; closing of eyes/mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat bodily signs (tears, fainting, paleness, smiles) as indicators that require contextual interpretation; they are not definitive proof of underlying states (see pp.50,73–76,89–96).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need, opportunity, motive and situational causes of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Need, and crime; Opportunity; Motives, apparent and real; Irritation causes crime; Sex as cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider situational and motivational factors (need, opportunity, motive, irritation, sexual factors) as explanatory variables in criminal behavior and as context when evaluating testimony (see pp.57–68, 322–323).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism as a corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism; and probability; and habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply healthy skepticism, informed by probability and habit effects, when weighing evidence and testimony (see pp.127–132).
